claims.statement: The pectoralis major has two heads: a clavicular head from the inner half of the collarbone and a sternocostal head from the breastbone, the upper six rib cartilages and the tendon sheet of the outer abdominal muscle. Acting apart, the clavicular head raises the arm forward (flexion) and the sternocostal head helps bring a raised arm back down (extension).

claims.statement: Bench-press studies measured upper-chest activity at different bench angles and do not fully agree. In 15 men pressing at four angles, the clavicular head was more active at inclines of 44 and 56 degrees than on a flat bench. In 30 trained adults, the upper portion of the muscle was most active at a 30-degree incline, and above 45 degrees front-deltoid activity rose while the pectoralis major's performance fell. In 14 trained men, upper-chest activity over the whole press did not differ between a 15-degree decline, a flat bench and inclines of 30 and 45 degrees, though both inclines gave more during part of the upward push. In an older study of 6 men, the clavicular head was no more active on an incline than on a flat bench, and less active on a decline. These are short-term activity measurements; they do not show which angle grows the muscle more.

No reference consulted calls the head a main extensor; those that grade its part say it contributes or facilitates, and an independent search described it as working with the latissimus dorsi, teres major and back of the deltoid, which most references treat as the main extensors. The head split does not need a prime row: the clavicular head carries flexion and this head extension either way. The shared action's description also covers moving the arm behind the body, which no source gives this head.
Elsevier says it 'assists in depressing'; StatPearls (thorax muscles) says it primarily depresses the shoulder; Kenhub says it can forcefully depress the scapula.

nodeActionsLeftOut.reason: Only one cited reference gives it, and as a possible action of the lowest fibres (wustl.serratus_anterior: 'may depress'; Brookbush and LearnMuscles, not cited, say the same); Kenhub summaries were inconsistent about which part pulls down. Left out under the forearm's rule for weak or disputed extras (03-anatomy-evidence.md §6); said in the function claim and a caveat.

Supported (Elsevier, Kenhub) but not a chest region action (§1.2; the back owns it). Said in the claim and a caveat. If the review wants it, the back's action id exists in §1.2 and the row would be 'assist'.

Parent node, neither drawn nor selectable (§1.2, §7.3): its actions are declared on the two heads, as the upper arm does for the triceps group. Second review: the shared test regionContent.test.ts:408-411 ('gives every muscle a main action, adjacent muscles aside') does not skip parents, and the pectoralis major is kind 'muscle', role 'group', so it fails as written; the lane or the platform adds a prime row here or exempts role 'group'.

UW and TeachMeAnatomy say the pectoralis major draws the scapula forward and down; it attaches to the upper-arm bone, not the shoulder blade, so the effect is through the arm. Listing it would offer the pectoralis major as a shoulder-blade target.
StatPearls says protraction 'allows for anteversion of the arm'; that is a shoulder-blade action that helps the arm forward, not a shoulder-joint action of the serratus.
Both can help lift ribs in forced breathing; there is no action id and it moves no load. Said in the pectoralis minor's claim.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Pectoralis Major
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q1, Q29, Q38): two heads, clavicular and sternocostal, named for their origins; the clavicular head flexes the extended arm; the sternocostal head's main work is adduction and medial rotation of the arm, plus extension of a flexed arm; the muscle sits beneath the breast tissue and forms the front wall of the armpit. The article's function list says 'Sternoclavicular head' where the sternocostal head is meant. Also served as statpearls.com point-of-care 26785. The search listing showed the title as 'Anatomy, Thorax, Pectoralis Major Major'; authors and update date were not shown. Second review (SR28): the Bookshelf listing confirms NBK525991 under the title 'Anatomy, Thorax, Pectoralis Major Major' (PubMed 30252247), by Francesca Solari and Bracken Burns, summarised as last updated 24 July 2023; the same summary gave the origin as the first seven costal cartilages, where TeachMeAnatomy, UW and IMAIOS say six (the claims cite those three for the number).

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Pectoral Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q28, Q29): the pectoral group (pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior, subclavius) flexes, adducts and internally rotates the humerus and stabilises the scapula; the pectoralis minor is thinner and triangular, beneath the pectoralis major, from the margins of the third to fifth ribs near the costochondral junction to the medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process, and is crucial in stabilising the scapula by pulling it down and forward against the chest wall. Also served as statpearls.com point-of-care 32427. A summary (Q11) attributed head-specific horizontal-adduction wording to StatPearls; a later search (Q62) found that wording is Wikipedia's, so this article is not cited for it. Authors not shown. Second review (SR28): the Bookshelf listing confirms NBK545241 under this title.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q28, one summary line only): the pectoralis minor primarily depresses the shoulder and protracts the scapula, and may assist inspiration by elevating the third, fourth and fifth ribs. Authors and date not shown. Second review (SR27, SR28): listed on Bookshelf under this title; PubMed 30855905.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Serratus Anterior Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30, Q32, Q35): fan-shaped, from the outer surfaces of the upper ribs (first to eighth in this article) to the superior angle, medial border and inferior angle of the scapula, in superior, intermediate and inferior parts; pulls the scapula forward around the thorax (protraction) and, with the upper and lower trapezius, sustains upward rotation of the scapula for overhead lifting; the inferior part rotates the scapula upward and gives the anterolateral motion that allows arm elevation; long thoracic nerve (C5 to C7); weakness causes a winged scapula. Also served as statpearls.com point-of-care 28922. Authors not shown.

sources.title: StatPearls: Winging of the Scapula
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30): medial scapular winging typically results from weakness of the serratus anterior, often caused by injury to the long thoracic nerve; lateral winging comes from trapezius or rhomboid dysfunction. Which StatPearls article each quoted sentence came from was not always named in the summary. Authors not shown.

sources.title: StatPearls: Poland Syndrome (archived)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q42): a set of anomalies that includes absence of the sternocostal head of the pectoralis major, often with pectoralis minor problems and syndactyly; defects are overwhelmingly one-sided. The excerpt stopped before the epidemiology section, so its incidence figure was not seen (other sources in the same results gave widely different figures). Authors not shown. Second review (SR25, SR27): Bookshelf and PubMed (30335292) list this article as 'Poland Syndrome (Archived)', by Dawood Tafti and Nathan D. Cecava, provided for historical reference; the maintained StatPearls article is 'Poland Syndrome in Children' (NBK560788), which no search excerpt was seen from. The claim also cites Radiopaedia and a clinical review for the same facts.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Mammary Gland
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q58): the gland extends vertically from the second to the sixth rib and from the side of the breastbone to the mid-axillary line; its base lies on the pectoral fascia over the pectoralis major. Used only for location. Authors not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: pectoralis major muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q2, Q11, Q38): as a whole the muscle adducts and internally rotates the arm at the shoulder; acting independently the clavicular part helps flex the extended arm up to 90 degrees, while the sternocostal part extends the flexed arm by pulling it downwards; in males it is covered by deep fascia, subcutaneous tissue and skin; the tendons of the two heads twist into an anterior (clavicular) and a posterior (sternocostal) lamina. A Kenhub video transcript says the muscle rotates the arm outwards, which conflicts with the written pages; the video is not cited.

sources.title: Kenhub: upper limb muscles and movements
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q2): the clavicular head makes the pectoralis major a flexor of the arm at the shoulder and the sternocostal head an extensor; acting as a unit the muscle is a medial rotator and adductor of the arm.

sources.title: Kenhub: glenohumeral (shoulder) joint
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q56): the prime flexors of the glenohumeral joint are the deltoid (anterior fibres) and the pectoralis major (clavicular fibres); adduction is produced by the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major, called the 'climbing muscles' as powerful adductors.

sources.title: Kenhub: pectoralis minor muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q24, Q31, Q41): lies deep only to the pectoralis major, which is its main front relation and almost completely covers it; from the third to fifth ribs to the coracoid process; protracts the scapula with the serratus anterior, can forcefully depress it, rotates it downward (medially), and with the scapula fixed helps raise ribs three to five in forced breathing. The summaries did not always say which Kenhub page (this one, the scapula page or the shoulder-girdle page) each action came from; innervation was given inconsistently and is not used.

sources.title: Kenhub: serratus anterior muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q31, Q35, Q37, Q40): a fan-shaped muscle on the side wall of the thorax whose main part lies deep under the scapula and the pectoral muscles; three parts, superior (ribs 1 to 2 to the superior angle), intermediate and inferior (ribs 4 to 8 or 9 to the medial border and inferior angle), the inferior part the most prominent and powerful; the whole muscle moves the scapula forward and sideways along the ribs and stabilises it; the inferior part's pull lets the arm be raised above 90 degrees; easy to palpate between the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, and in athletic bodies may be visible along the ribs underneath the axilla. One summary (Q31) said the superior part pulls the scapula downward; the German Kenhub page (Q35) says the superior part elevates the scapula and lowers the glenoid. Neither is used for an action.

sources.title: Kenhub: trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q31): upward rotation of the scapula is shared between the trapezius and the serratus anterior. Cited only for that statement.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: pectoralis major
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q3, Q11): adducts, medially rotates and transversely adducts the arm at the shoulder joint; the clavicular head assists flexion of the arm. No extension listed. Second review (SR3, SR5): summaries disagree on extension. One quoted the page as 'assists in extension of the arm at the glenohumeral joint via its sternocostal head'; another said the snippet stopped before any extension wording; the first pass saw none. The claims therefore cite this page for transverse adduction and the clavicular head's assisting flexion only, not for extension either way.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: pectoralis minor
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q25): from the anterior ends of the third to fifth ribs to the coracoid process; protracts the shoulder girdle, downwardly rotates it and assists in depressing it; may act as an accessory muscle of inspiration.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: serratus anterior
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q33, Q37): from the outer surfaces of the first to ninth ribs to the medial border of the scapula; long thoracic nerve (C5 to C7); protracts the shoulder girdle and rotates it upward, and helps stabilise the scapula against the thoracic wall (attributed to Standring 2016); lies superficial to the first eight ribs and external intercostals, deep to the scapula, latissimus dorsi, trapezius and subscapularis, and behind the pectoralis major and minor.

sources.title: IMAIOS e-Anatomy: pectoralis major muscle

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: muscles of the pectoral region
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q8, Q27, Q38; with the site's encyclopaedia pages on the pectoralis major and minor, which gave the same facts): the pectoralis major is the most superficial muscle of the pectoral region, fan-shaped, with a clavicular head from the front of the medial clavicle and a sternocostal head from the sternum, the upper six costal cartilages and the external oblique aponeurosis, both attaching at the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus; it adducts and medially rotates the arm and draws the scapula forward and down, and the clavicular head acting alone flexes the arm. sources.title: Radiopaedia: pectoralis major muscle

sources.title: Radiopaedia: serratus anterior muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q37; seen through the images.radiopaedia.org mirror, partial text only): from the lateral surfaces of the first to eighth or ninth ribs to the medial border of the scapula; long thoracic nerve; injury to that nerve in armpit surgery causes winging because the muscle no longer holds the scapula against the chest wall.

sources.title: Lulic-Kuryllo, Negro, Jiang and Dickerson, Differential regional pectoralis major activation indicates functional diversity in healthy females (Journal of Biomechanics 133:110966, 2022)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q13, Q15, Q21; abstract, the UWSpace accepted manuscript record and the PubMed record): high-density surface EMG of the clavicular, superior sternocostal and middle sternocostal regions in 29 healthy young women, two experiments, ramp-and-hold isometric tasks at several force levels. The middle sternocostal region was 12 to 108 per cent more active than the other two regions in extension, adduction with external rotation and high-elevation internal rotation; in forward and horizontal flexion the three regions were similar at every force level except forward flexion at 25 per cent of maximal force, where the clavicular region was 21 per cent more active than the superior sternocostal region; in low-elevation internal rotation the clavicular and middle sternocostal regions were more active than the superior sternocostal region. Acute isometric activity in women only, not growth. Second review (SR12): an independent summary of the UWSpace record and abstract agreed, including high-density surface EMG and 29 women.

sources.title: Trebs, Brandenburg and Pitney, An electromyography analysis of 3 muscles surrounding the shoulder joint during the performance of a chest press exercise at several angles (Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 24(7):1925–1930, 2010)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q18, Q20, Q22; abstract as summarised): 15 healthy men pressed at 0, 28, 44 and 56 degrees above horizontal with seven tenths of their one-repetition maximum. Clavicular-head activity was greater at 44 and 56 degrees than flat and at 44 than 28 degrees; sternocostal activity was greater flat than at each incline and greater at 28 and 44 than at 56 degrees; anterior deltoid activity was greater at every incline than flat. The PubMed id was not confirmed (20508462, suggested in a query, is a different study). Second review (SR7): an independent summary confirmed the citation, the 15 healthy men, the four angles, seven tenths of one-repetition maximum and the clavicular-head comparisons; it did not show the sternocostal results, which rest on the first pass's two summaries. PubMed id still not confirmed.

sources.title: Rodríguez-Ridao et al., Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(19):7339, 2020)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q17, Q20; abstract; full text at PMC7579505): 30 trained adults pressed at 0, 15, 30, 45 and 60 degrees at six tenths of one-repetition maximum, with EMG of three portions of the pectoralis major, the anterior deltoid and the triceps. The upper portion was most active at 30 degrees; the middle and lower portions at 0 degrees; the anterior deltoid at 60 degrees; above 45 degrees anterior deltoid activation rose and pectoralis major performance fell. The abstract names an upper portion, not the clavicular head. DOI not shown in the results. Full author list not shown. Second review (SR8): an independent summary agreed on every result above and gave the DOI 10.3390/ijerph17197339.

sources.title: Barnett, Kippers and Turner, Effects of variations of the bench press exercise on the EMG activity of five shoulder muscles (Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 9(4):222–227, 1995)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q19; library-record abstract, one summary): six male weight trainers pressed at four trunk inclinations and two hand spacings at eight tenths of their maximum. The sternocostal head was more active on a flat bench than on a decline; the clavicular head was no more active on an incline than flat, less active on a decline, and more active with a narrow hand spacing; anterior deltoid activity tended to rise with inclination. The record lists the authors as Kippers, Turner and Barnett; citing papers put Barnett first. PubMed id and DOI not seen. Second review (SR9): a second summary of the same record agreed with every result above. It added that the 2020 bench-angle paper (PMC7579505) describes Barnett and colleagues' sternocostal comparison as flat against incline, not flat against decline; the claims follow the abstract (decline).

sources.title: Castelein, Cagnie, Parlevliet and Cools, Serratus anterior or pectoralis minor: Which muscle has the upper hand during protraction exercises? (Manual Therapy 22:158–164, 2016)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q50, Q52, Q54; abstract as summarised twice): 26 healthy subjects performed a wall and a floor (knee) modified push-up plus and a serratus punch, with surface EMG of the serratus anterior and fine-wire EMG of the pectoralis minor. In the serratus punch serratus activity was significantly higher than pectoralis minor activity; in both push-up plus versions the two were comparable; all exercises activated the pectoralis minor at 15 to 29 and the serratus at 15 to 43 per cent of maximal voluntary isometric contraction. A letter to the editor (PubMed 27133020) was not read. DOI not shown. Second review (SR17): an independent summary of the PubMed, ScienceDirect and ResearchGate records agreed with every result above.

sources.title: GPnotebook: serratus anterior, anatomy and testing
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q32, Q36, Q39): the digitations are often seen and felt on the side wall of the chest, particularly in young, athletic subjects, and a wall push or press-up brings them out; the first digitation arises from the first and second ribs; the lowest four digitations interlock with the costal attachments of the external oblique. theHeadSplit: Supported by the function claims. Head-specific actions are named by StatPearls (NBK525991), Kenhub (two pages), IMAIOS, the UW atlas, TeachMeAnatomy and the PMC case report: the clavicular head flexes the arm, the sternocostal head extends a flexed arm; together they adduct and turn the arm inward. Loyola names no extension, and Elsevier calls the clavicular head's flexion 'assisting': the claims say so. Second review: the sternocostal head's extension is now 'assist' (references say it contributes or facilitates); the split does not depend on that role.

Muscle-activity evidence supports half of the split clearly. In isometric tasks (pmid.35093733) the middle sternocostal region was much more active than the clavicular region in extension and in adduction with the arm turned out, but in forward and horizontal flexion the three regions were about equally active, except forward pushing at a quarter of maximal force, where the clavicular region was more active than the upper sternocostal region. Bench-press studies disagree on whether an incline raises clavicular activity (lww.chest_press_angles yes at 44 and 56 degrees; pmid.33049982 most at 30 degrees; bisp.bench_press_five_shoulder_muscles no; pmid.25799093 no difference over the whole press, more at 30 and 45 degrees during part of it). The split therefore stands on anatomy, and the claims say that the forward-raising difference is not a measured difference in activity. The atlas resting the clavicular head's forward-raising action on anatomy references is an accounting choice; the second review moved that sentence out of the selectivity claim and into this note.
